claim: TAP is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter essential to cellular immunity against viral infection.
source: The transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter essential to cellular immunity against viral infection.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about TAP's role.

claim: Herpes simplex virus evades immune surveillance by blocking peptide transport with ICP47.
source: The herpes simplex virus for example evades immune surveillance by blocking peptide transport with a small viral protein ICP47.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of human TAP bound to ICP47 was determined by cryo-EM to 4.0 Å resolution.
source: In this study, we determined the structure of human TAP bound to ICP47 by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) to 4.0 Å.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the study, supported by the cryo-EM data and reconstruction shown in Figure 1.

claim: ICP47 traps TAP in an inactive conformation distinct from the normal transport cycle.
source: The structure shows that ICP47 traps TAP in an inactive conformation distinct from the normal transport cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis comparing TAP/ICP47 to other ABC transporters.

claim: The specificity and potency of ICP47 inhibition result from contacts between the tip of the helical hairpin and the apex of the transmembrane cavity.
source: The specificity and potency of ICP47 inhibition result from contacts between the tip of the helical hairpin and the apex of the transmembrane cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis data discussed in the results.

claim: Cytotoxic T cells detect and eliminate infected cells by recognizing viral peptides displayed on the cell surface by MHC-I molecules.
source: Cytotoxic T cells detect and eliminate infected cells by recognizing viral peptides displayed on the cell surface by major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I) molecules (Blum et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the ER lumen.
source: The transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) transports these cytosolic peptides into the ER lumen, where a multi-component peptide-loading complex facilitates peptide-binding to nascent MHC-I molecules (Neefjes et al., 1993; Shepherd et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TAP-deficient cells have reduced surface expression of MHC-I molecules and are less sensitive to cytotoxic T cells.
source: TAP-deficient cells have a reduced surface expression of MHC-I molecules and are less sensitive to cytotoxic T cells (Deverson et al., 1990; Monaco et al., 1990; Spies et al., 1990; Trowsdale et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: TAP is formed by two homologous subunits, TAP1 and TAP2.
source: TAP is an ER-resident transporter formed by two homologous subunits, TAP1 and TAP2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TAP structure.

claim: TAP contains two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) that hydrolyze ATP and two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that bind the substrate.
source: Similar to other ABC transporters, it contains two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) that hydrolyze ATP and two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that bind the substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of TAP similar to other ABC transporters.

claim: Both TAP1 and TAP2 contain an N-terminal transmembrane region (TMD0) that interacts with tapasin to form the larger peptide-loading complex.
source: In addition, both TAP1 and TAP2 contain an N-terminal transmembrane region (TMD0) that interacts with tapasin to form the larger peptide-loading complex (Hulpke et al., 2012; Procko et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TAP's broad substrate specificity is one of the most important properties for its function.
source: TAP's broad substrate specificity is one of the most important properties for its function (Androlewicz and Cresswell, 1994; Momburg et al., 1994a; Neefjes et al., 1995; van Endert et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Humans typically express six different MHC-I molecules, each binding to a large variety of peptides.
source: Humans typically express six different MHC-I molecules, each binding to a large variety of peptides and conferring a different specificity (Falk et al., 1991; Hunt et al., 1992; Jardetzky et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The same TAP transporter provides peptides for all six MHC-I molecules.
source: The same TAP transporter provides peptides for all six MHC-I molecules; therefore, it must be more promiscuous than any single MHC-I molecule.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of TAP's role in the antigen presentation pathway.

claim: Human TAP has a preference for a hydrophobic or basic residue at the C-terminus of peptide substrates.
source: The only sequence constraint found for human TAP is a preference for a hydrophobic or basic residue at the C-terminus (Momburg et al., 1994b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: TAP's peptide preference complements MHC-I specificity in that an acidic C-terminus is rarely seen in MHC-I presented peptides.
source: Interestingly, this peptide preference complements MHC-I specificity in that an acidic C-terminus is rarely seen in MHC-I presented peptides (Rammensee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: TAP can transport peptides up to 40 residues long.
source: Despite its ability to transport a diverse range of peptides up to 40 residues long (Momburg et al., 1994a), TAP is still subject to inhibition by some viral peptides.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Human herpes simplex virus (HSV) encodes the potent TAP inhibitor ICP47.
source: For example, human herpes simplex virus (HSV) encodes the potent TAP inhibitor ICP47 (Früh et al., 1995; Hill et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Peptides containing the N-terminal 34 residues of ICP47 are sufficient to bind TAP and prevent peptide translocation.
source: Peptides containing the N-terminal 34 residues of ICP47 are sufficient to bind TAP and prevent peptide translocation (Galocha et al., 1997; Neumann et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Suppressing the presentation of viral peptides renders HSV-infected cells undetectable to cytotoxic T cells.
source: Suppressing the presentation of viral peptides renders HSV-infected cells undetectable to cytotoxic T cells (York et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: A previous structure of the TAP/ICP47 complex was determined at 6.5 Å resolution using cryo-EM.
source: Previously, we determined the structure of a TAP/ICP47 complex using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Oldham et al., 2016). This structure, at 6.5 Å resolution, showed that the N-terminal region of ICP47 forms a helical hairpin, inserting itself into TAP's substrate translocation pathway.
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: The N-terminal region of ICP47 forms a helical hairpin that inserts into TAP's substrate translocation pathway.
source: This structure, at 6.5 Å resolution, showed that the N-terminal region of ICP47 forms a helical hairpin, inserting itself into TAP's substrate translocation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by the previous structural study and confirmed by the current higher resolution structure.

claim: The ordered region of the TAP/ICP47 complex has a molecular mass of 130 kDa.
source: As the ordered region of the TAP/ICP47 complex has a molecular mass of only 130 kDa and exhibits a pseudo-twofold symmetry, two factors likely limiting resolution are the accuracy with which the noisy cryo-EM images of single particles can be aligned and the ability to distinguish pseudo-symmetrically related views.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the complex that affects resolution.

claim: The TAP/ICP47 complex exhibits pseudo-twofold symmetry.
source: As the ordered region of the TAP/ICP47 complex has a molecular mass of only 130 kDa and exhibits a pseudo-twofold symmetry, two factors likely limiting resolution are the accuracy with which the noisy cryo-EM images of single particles can be aligned and the ability to distinguish pseudo-symmetrically related views.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the complex that affects resolution.

claim: Higher magnification reduced the effective pixel size from 1.35 Å to 1.04 Å.
source: The higher magnification reduced the effective pixel size of the images from 1.35 Å used in our previous study to 1.04 Å (Table 1), boosting the detective quantum efficiency (DQE) of the K2 Summit detector (Gatan, Inc.) at 7 Å resolution by about 6% (Li et al., 2013; McMullan et al., 2009; Ruskin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the data collection parameters in Table 1.

claim: Higher magnification boosted the detective quantum efficiency (DQE) of the K2 Summit detector at 7 Å resolution by about 6%.
source: The higher magnification reduced the effective pixel size of the images from 1.35 Å used in our previous study to 1.04 Å (Table 1), boosting the detective quantum efficiency (DQE) of the K2 Summit detector (Gatan, Inc.) at 7 Å resolution by about 6% (Li et al., 2013; McMullan et al., 2009; Ruskin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on detector performance.

claim: The best result for specimen movement correction was obtained by whole frame alignment followed by individual particle tracking.
source: The best result was obtained by whole frame alignment followed by individual particle tracking. This combination of methods also works best for other small particles such as the γ-secretase (Bai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological finding from comparing different processing approaches.

claim: The final reconstruction has an average resolution of 4.0 Å.
source: The final reconstruction has an average resolution of 4.0 Å (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is the primary result of the cryo-EM reconstruction, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The TM region is better resolved than the two NBDs.
source: Analyzing regional variations in resolution using the program Blocres (Cardone et al., 2013) indicates that the TM region is better resolved than the two NBDs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown by local resolution analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: The density map for ICP47 and the TMDs of TAP shows prominent side chain density sufficient to register the amino acid identity.
source: The density map for ICP47 and the TMDs of TAP shows prominent side chain density sufficient to register the amino acid identity (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is shown in the density maps in Figure 1.

claim: The density corresponding to the two NBDs is adequate to assign secondary structure but lacks side chain definition.
source: The density corresponding to the two NBDs is adequate to assign secondary structure but lacks side chain definition (Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed in the density maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: The model contains the 12 core TM-helices of TAP and the N-terminal 55 residues of ICP47.
source: With this map, we built and refined a model containing the 12 core TM-helices of TAP and the N-terminal 55 residues of ICP47 (Table 2).
evidence: This describes the content of the structural model built from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The TAP structure has the canonical fold of ABC exporters.
source: The TAP structure has the canonical fold of ABC exporters (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the structure presented in Figure 2.

claim: The 12 transmembrane helices at the core are arranged into two bundles, each consisting of TM 1–3 and 6 of one subunit and TM 4–5 of the other subunit.
source: The 12 transmembrane (TM) helices at the core are arranged into two bundles, each consisting of TM 1–3 and 6 of one subunit and TM 4–5 of the other subunit (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the domain-swapped architecture shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The NBDs are attached to each TM bundle at their cytoplasmic ends and are separated from each other.
source: The NBDs are attached to each TM bundle at their cytoplasmic ends and are separated from each other.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The N-terminal 55 residues of ICP47 form a helical hairpin structure that inserts into the opening between the two TM bundles.
source: The N-terminal 55 residues of ICP47 form a helical hairpin structure, which inserts into the opening between the two TM bundles.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: No density was observed for the C-terminal 33 residues of ICP47 or the two TMD0s.
source: No density was observed for either the C-terminal 33 residues of ICP47 or the two TMD0s, indicating these regions are flexible in this conformation.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The C-terminal 33 residues of ICP47 and the two TMD0s are flexible in this conformation.
source: No density was observed for either the C-terminal 33 residues of ICP47 or the two TMD0s, indicating these regions are flexible in this conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: In the TAP/ICP47 structure, the gating region is cracked open by ICP47 to a width approximately 4 Å in diameter.
source: In TAP, however, this gating region is cracked open by ICP47 to a width approximately 4 Å in diameter (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A lateral opening to the membrane leaflet is observed near the ER lumen side in the TAP/ICP47 structure.
source: In addition, a lateral opening to the membrane leaflet is observed near the ER lumen side (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ER openings observed in the structure of TAP/ICP47 complex are most likely induced by ICP47.
source: Therefore, it is most likely that the ER openings observed in the structure of TAP/ICP47 complex are induced by ICP47.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and the alternating access model.

claim: A functional TAP without inhibitor would presumably open the TM pathway to only one side of the membrane at a time to avoid potential ion leakage across the ER membrane.
source: A functional TAP without inhibitor would presumably open the TM pathway to only one side of the membrane at a time to avoid potential ion leakage across the ER membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the alternating access model and the observation of openings in the inhibited structure.

claim: ICP47 competes with substrates for the same binding pocket.
source: Although we do not yet have direct structural data regarding where or how natural substrates bind, there is strong evidence suggesting that ICP47 competes with substrates for the same binding pocket (Ahn et al., 1996; Früh et al., 1995; Hill et al., 1995; Tomazin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Residues 375–420 and 453–487 in TAP1 and 301–389 and 414–433 in TAP2 are part of the substrate binding site.
source: Studies using radiolabeled peptides and mass spectrometry identified four regions, residues 375–420 and 453–487 in TAP1 and 301–389 and 414–433 in TAP2, as part of the binding site (Nijenhuis and Hämmerling, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to biochemical studies.

claim: The substrate-binding regions identified biochemically are part of the TM helices enclosing the large internal cavity.
source: Mapping these residues onto the structure shows that they are part of the TM helices enclosing the large internal cavity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by mapping biochemical data onto the structure in Figure 3A.

claim: The electrostatic environment of the TM cavity provides an appropriate interface for binding peptides with free N- and C-termini.
source: The electrostatic environment of the TM cavity containing strong positively and negatively charged patches provides an appropriate interface for binding peptides with free N- and C-termini (Figure 3B) (Momburg et al., 1994b; Schumacher et al., 1994).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Many residues identified by mutagenesis or substrate crosslinking experiments are located on the surface of the TM cavity.
source: Many residues identified by mutagenesis or substrate crosslinking experiments are located on the surface of this cavity (Figure 3A and C) (Armandola et al., 1996; Deverson et al., 1998; Geng et al., 2015; Momburg et al., 1996).
evidence: This is shown by mapping functional data onto the structure in Figure 3.

claim: In the TAP/ICP47 complex, residues identified by mutagenesis are buried by ICP47.
source: In the TAP/ICP47 complex these residues are buried by ICP47, consistent with data showing that ICP47 precludes peptide binding (Ahn et al., 1996; Früh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and consistent with functional data.

claim: Y408 of TAP1 and M218 of TAP2 are proposed to serve as anchors for the C-termini of bound peptides.
source: Interestingly, the two residues proposed to serve as anchors for the C-termini of bound peptides, Y408 of TAP1 and M218 of TAP2 (Geng et al., 2015; Momburg et al., 1996), both interact with the N-terminal region of ICP47 through van der Waals contacts (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Y408 of TAP1 and M218 of TAP2 interact with the N-terminal region of ICP47 through van der Waals contacts.
source: Interestingly, the two residues proposed to serve as anchors for the C-termini of bound peptides, Y408 of TAP1 and M218 of TAP2 (Geng et al., 2015; Momburg et al., 1996), both interact with the N-terminal region of ICP47 through van der Waals contacts (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Substrates interact with TAP through a very different mode from that of ICP47.
source: This observation is consistent with our previous suggestion that substrates interact with TAP through a very different mode from that of ICP47 (Oldham et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and cited from previous work.

claim: 32 residues from ICP47 and 36 residues from TAP come into direct contact at the interface.
source: The interaction surface between ICP47 and TAP is extensive: 32 residues from ICP47 and 36 residues from TAP come into direct contact at the interface.
evidence: This is measured from the structure.

claim: The solvent-accessible surface area of TAP buried by ICP47 is 2360 Å2.
source: The solvent-accessible surface area of TAP buried by ICP47 is 2360 Å2 (Figure 4A), which is twice the average binding surface between proteins in general (London et al., 2010) and four times the surface area of an MHC-I molecule buried by a peptide antigen (Rudolph et al., 2002).
evidence: This is calculated from the structure and compared to literature values.

claim: The buried surface area between TAP and ICP47 is twice the average binding surface between proteins in general.
source: The solvent-accessible surface area of TAP buried by ICP47 is 2360 Å2 (Figure 4A), which is twice the average binding surface between proteins in general (London et al., 2010) and four times the surface area of an MHC-I molecule buried by a peptide antigen (Rudolph et al., 2002).
evidence: This is calculated from the structure and compared to a cited literature value.

claim: The buried surface area between TAP and ICP47 is four times the surface area of an MHC-I molecule buried by a peptide antigen.
source: The solvent-accessible surface area of TAP buried by ICP47 is 2360 Å2 (Figure 4A), which is twice the average binding surface between proteins in general (London et al., 2010) and four times the surface area of an MHC-I molecule buried by a peptide antigen (Rudolph et al., 2002).
evidence: This is calculated from the structure and compared to a cited literature value.

claim: The N-terminal 34 residues of ICP47 are largely buried inside the translocation pathway, forming a helical bundle with TAP2 TM helices 3 and 6.
source: The N-terminal 34 residues of ICP47 are largely buried inside the translocation pathway, forming a helical bundle with TAP2 TM helices 3 and 6 (Figure 3C and 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figures 3C and 4C.

claim: Contact between the N-terminal 34 residues of ICP47 and TAP is sufficient to prevent substrate binding and subsequent conformational changes associated with transport.
source: Previous studies suggest that this contact alone is sufficient to prevent substrate binding and subsequent conformational changes associated with transport (Galocha et al., 1997; Neumann et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Residues 35–55 of ICP47 pack closely along TAP2 TM3 and make contact with IH1.
source: Residues 35–55 of ICP47 continue to pack closely along TAP2 TM3 and make contact with IH1 (intracellular helix 1), a coupling helix at the TMD/NBD interface.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: P55 of ICP47 interacts with Y477 of TAP, which normally makes an aromatic stacking interaction with the adenine ring of ATP.
source: The last ordered residue of ICP47, P55, interacts with Y477, which normally makes an aromatic stacking interaction with the adenine ring of ATP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutations at positions 18 to 25 of ICP47 that reduced activity by more than 50% are located in the region where the two helices are connected by a sharp turn.
source: Mutations that reduced the activity by more than 50% are located in one region, from positions 18 to 25, where the two helices are connected by a sharp turn (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on functional data cited from literature and mapped onto the structure.

claim: A 'turn-to-helix' mutant replacing residues 16–22 with alanine reduced the activity of ICP47 by a factor of five.
source: Previously, we generated a 'turn-to-helix' mutant by replacing residues in the same region (16–22) with alanine (Oldham et al., 2016). This mutant, predicted to have a higher propensity to form a long alpha-helix rather than the hairpin structure, indeed reduced the activity of ICP47 by a factor of five (Oldham et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: ICP47 from HSV inhibits TAP in human, monkey, pig, cow and dog cells, but not in rabbit, mouse and rat cells.
source: Previous studies showed that ICP47 from HSV inhibits TAP in human, monkey, pig, cow and dog cells, but not in rabbit, mouse and rat cells (Ahn et al., 1996; Jugovic et al., 1998; Verweij et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Residues that are highly conserved in ICP47-sensitive species but not in rabbit, mouse and rat are located near the apex of the TM cavity.
source: When we map these residues onto the human TAP/ICP47 structure we observe that all but one of them are located near the apex of the TM cavity, interacting with the 'hot spot' residues in ICP47 that were identified in the alanine scan (Figure 4C) (Galocha et al., 1997).
evidence: This is shown by sequence analysis and mapping onto the structure in Figure 4C.

claim: Amino acid changes near the apex of the TM cavity account for TAP susceptibility to ICP47 among different species.
source: Thus, it appears that in the setting of a very large interface between TAP and ICP47, amino acid changes in this region are particularly important and account for TAP susceptibility to ICP47 among the species analyzed here.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis and structural mapping.

claim: The T425N substitution in mouse and rat is incompatible with the close contacts between T425 and F11 and Y22 of ICP47.
source: For example, both mouse and rat contain a T425N substitution, which is incompatible with the close contacts between T425 and F11 and Y22 of ICP47 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure shown in Figure 4D and sequence analysis.

claim: Substituting F11 or Y22 of ICP47 with alanine reduced inhibition by 40% and 60% respectively.
source: Substituting F11 or Y22 with alanine reduced lCP47 inhibition by 40% and 60% respectively (Galocha et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claim: The lack of ICP47 inhibition in rabbit cells can be explained by the substitution of S421 with arginine.
source: The lack of ICP47 inhibition in rabbit cells can be explained by the substitution of S421 with the large, charged arginine residue, which probably prevents insertion of the helical hairpin into the top of TM cavity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis and the structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutagenesis to identify functional hotspots on ICP47 and analysis of specificity determinants on TAP both point to the same molecular interface at the tip of the helical hairpin as being crucial to ICP47 inhibition.
source: Therefore, two independent approaches—mutagenesis to identify functional hotspots on ICP47 (Galocha et al., 1997) and analysis of specificity determinants on TAP—both point to the same molecular interface at the tip of the helical hairpin as being crucial to the action of ICP47 to inhibit TAP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from combining functional data and structural analysis.

claim: TAP transports peptide antigens into the ER through conformational changes powered by ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: TAP transports peptide antigens into the ER through conformational changes powered by ATP binding and hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated as part of the mechanism discussion, based on knowledge of ABC transporters.

claim: In the absence of substrate and ATP, TAP rests in an inward-facing conformation in which the two NBDs are separated and the translocation pathway faces the cytoplasm.
source: Based on what we have learned from homologous ABC transporters, we can envision that in the absence of substrate and ATP, TAP rests in an inward-facing conformation in which the two NBDs are separated and the translocation pathway faces the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of ABC transporter mechanisms.

claim: Upon binding to substrate and ATP, the two NBDs of TAP form a closed dimer and the translocation pathway orients towards the ER lumen to release the peptide.
source: Upon binding to the substrate and ATP, the two NBDs form a closed dimer and the translocation pathway orients towards the ER lumen to release the peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of ABC transporter mechanisms.

claim: ATP hydrolysis at the closed NBD dimer interface resets TAP to its resting state.
source: ATP hydrolysis at the closed NBD dimer interface resets TAP to its resting state, ready for the next transport cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of ABC transporter mechanisms.

claim: ICP47 precludes substrate binding by inserting a long helical hairpin into the translocation pathway.
source: ICP47 precludes substrate binding by inserting a long helical hairpin into the translocation pathway.
evidence: This is observed in the structure and supported by functional data.

claim: The strong interaction between ICP47 and TAP traps TAP in an inward-facing conformation with the two NBDs separated.
source: The strong interaction between ICP47 and TAP traps TAP in an inward-facing conformation with the two NBDs separated, unable to progress to the NBD-closed conformation necessary for ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is observed in the structure and inferred from the mechanism.

claim: ICP47 prevents TAP from progressing to the NBD-closed conformation necessary for ATP hydrolysis.
source: The strong interaction between ICP47 and TAP traps TAP in an inward-facing conformation with the two NBDs separated, unable to progress to the NBD-closed conformation necessary for ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and knowledge of ABC transporter mechanisms.

claim: By blocking translocation of viral peptides into the ER, HSV suppresses the MHC-I antigen presentation pathway and escapes cytotoxic T cell detection.
source: By blocking translocation of viral peptides into the ER, HSV suppresses the MHC-I antigen presentation pathway and thereby escapes cytotoxic T cell detection.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion about the mechanism of immune evasion, based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Crystal structures were determined for E. coli McjD in the AMPPNP-bound conformation.
source: Previously, crystal structures were determined for two prokaryotic peptide transporters: the E. coli McjD in the AMPPNP-bound conformation (pdb: 4PL0) (Choudhury et al., 2014; Mehmood et al., 2016) and the peptidase-containing ABC transporter from Clostridium thermocellum (PCAT1) in two different conformations (inward-facing pdb: 4RY2; occluded, ATPγS-bound pdb: 4S0F) (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structures.

claim: Crystal structures were determined for PCAT1 in two different conformations (inward-facing and occluded, ATPγS-bound).
source: Previously, crystal structures were determined for two prokaryotic peptide transporters: the E. coli McjD in the AMPPNP-bound conformation (pdb: 4PL0) (Choudhury et al., 2014; Mehmood et al., 2016) and the peptidase-containing ABC transporter from Clostridium thermocellum (PCAT1) in two different conformations (inward-facing pdb: 4RY2; occluded, ATPγS-bound pdb: 4S0F) (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structures.

claim: TAP is a promiscuous transporter found only in jawed vertebrates.
source: Unlike TAP, which is a promiscuous transporter found only in jawed vertebrates (Hinz et al., 2014), McjD and PCAT1 are dedicated to specific substrates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature.

claim: McjD exports microcin J25, a 21-residue antibacterial peptide with a lasso fold.
source: McjD exports microcin J25, a 21-residue antibacterial peptide with a lasso fold.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about McjD function.

claim: PCAT1 functions both as a maturation protease and exporter for a 90-residue peptide with an amino-terminal leader sequence.
source: PCAT1 functions both as a maturation protease and exporter for a 90-residue peptide with an amino-terminal leader sequence.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PCAT1 function.

claim: PCAT1 contains two peptidase domains in addition to the canonical TMDs and NBDs.
source: Correspondingly, PCAT1 contains two peptidase domains in addition to the canonical TMDs and NBDs.
evidence: This is stated as a structural feature of PCAT1.

claim: TAP, PCAT1, and McjD share a similar fold in the core region.
source: Despite these differences, the three transporters share a similar fold in the core region: the NBDs have very similar structures and the TM helices in each subunit are of similar length with a similar trajectory (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown by structural comparison in Figure 6.

claim: In TAP, TM 4-5 appears to be pushed outward and bent compared to PCAT1 and McjD.
source: One notable difference between TAP and the other two transporters occurs in TM 4-5, which in TAP appears to be pushed outward and bent (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The difference in TM 4-5 could possibly reflect a distortion due to the presence of ICP47.
source: This difference, however, could possibly reflect a distortion due to the presence of ICP47.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observation.

claim: TAP shows the largest separation between the two halves compared to PCAT1 and McjD.
source: The overall structures of TAP, PCAT1, and McjD differ in the separation of the two halves, reflecting the different conformational states each structure represents. TAP shows the largest separation, again possibly induced by the viral inhibitor ICP47.
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison.

claim: The large separation in TAP is possibly induced by the viral inhibitor ICP47.
source: TAP shows the largest separation, again possibly induced by the viral inhibitor ICP47.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observation.

claim: The two NBDs of PCAT1 form a semi-open dimer in the absence of a nucleotide.
source: The two NBDs of PCAT1 form a semi-open dimer in the absence of a nucleotide, separated at the TMD/NBD interfaces and making contacts at the distal end of the structure (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the PCAT1 structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the presence of ATP analogs and the absence of substrate, both McjD and PCAT1 reveal an occluded conformation.
source: In the presence of ATP analogs and the absence of a substrate, both McjD and PCAT1 reveal an occluded conformation in which the NBDs are closed and the translocation pathway is shielded from both sides of the membrane (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the structures shown in Figure 6.

claim: The similarity in structures of TAP, PCAT1, and McjD suggests they may share a common evolutionary origin and a common mechanism for coupling ATP hydrolysis to peptide translocation.
source: The similarity in their structures suggests that these transporters may share a common evolutionary origin and a common mechanism for coupling ATP hydrolysis to peptide translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities observed.

claim: The best results for movement correction were obtained by combining whole frame alignment with subsequent individual particle tracking.
source: Using these three different procedures, the best resolution values obtained at the stage of AutoRefine3D in Relion were 7.5 Å, 7.4 Å, and 6.6 Å, respectively. Thus, the best results were obtained by combining whole frame alignment with subsequent individual particle tracking.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from comparing different processing approaches.

claim: All 502,000 particles that were automatically extracted from the micrographs were used for the 3D reconstruction.
